toc.title: The present moment and all it brings

blocks.p: Once you're grounding yourself in safety with [Cue to Anchor](piece:cue-to-anchor), recognizing your internal world with [Validating & Normalizing](piece:validating-and-normalizing), and gently welcoming your emotions with [Imagery & Invitation](piece:imagery-and-invitation), you're making excellent progress.

As you continue this inward journey and practice these skills, something interesting (and sometimes frustrating!) is likely to happen: other experiences will emerge that you didn't expect or ask for. (Maybe you've noticed this already?) These are what I call Obstacles. But, spoiler alert, they're not really obstacles…

Think of Obstacles as unexpected visitors that appear during your mindful practice. They're internal experiences (Sensations, Impulses, Emotions, Cognitions) that surface and likely disrupt your focus.

Obstacles will surface, not a matter of if, but when. They will happen. When they do, and you struggle with them, remember that they don't define you, your worth, or your potential. They aren't signs that you're "doing it wrong" or that you're broken. They are simply part of the process.

Obstacles indicate that your vagal brake might be releasing. You may have reached a point where defense is increasing beyond what your safety state can accommodate. As safety releases, the vagal brake also releases, resulting in increased defensive activation. As defense rises, various SSIECs will naturally emerge in your conscious experience. This isn't necessarily dysregulation, but it could lean into it.

This is expected. It simply shows that your safety state needs strengthening. Obstacles appearing and the release of your vagal brake are signs of your current tolerance level. This information is helpful and points to where you should focus your efforts. Instead of forcing yourself into more challenging emotional content or new skills, you'll concentrate on what is within your tolerance and skill levels.

Obstacles are not necessarily dysregulation, but they could be. They might also indicate that dysregulation is approaching. So, notice the Obstacle and its intensity early, then decide to pause the practice and recover. If dysregulation occurs, it will show up as the [four signs that it's time to stop](piece:starting-and-stopping#when-to-stop).

I'll reiterate: Obstacles are not signs of failure. They are a normal part of the process and temporary. As you practice anchoring in safety and welcoming defense through the Skills you've already learned, your vagal brake strengthens and distress tolerance grows. As it does, your ability to notice and welcome Obstacles also grows.

Instead of ignoring, battling, or pushing through Obstacles, you will approach them more mindfully and compassionately. This will further reduce their intensity, strengthen your safety state, and enhance your ability to notice and welcome more Obstacles. This process gradually peels back layer after layer of defensive SSIEC.
Obstacles can appear as any of your defensive SSIEC. You will likely notice them most obviously as Cognitions. Cognitive obstacles can sound like:

These are just a handful of examples of Cognitive Obstacles. Your Obstacles and how they show up will be unique to you, your history, and your current circumstances. Trust me, Obstacles can take many forms and vary in intensity. As you practice, you'll get much better at noticing Obstacles early, when they are smallest and easiest to handle.

As best we can, we intentionally welcome and spend time with Obstacles mindfully. An obstacle is an opportunity. If you treat it disrespectfully, you're depriving yourself of valuable chances for healing. If you approach it with compassion, you're giving yourself the chance to peel back layers of defensive SSIEC. If you can do that, your stuck defense gradually shifts. You become more self-regulated.

Remember our ideal meditative goal? To connect with the present moment, whatever it brings. Obstacles are opportunities because they are the most immediate experience. If the present moment brings you a hint of anxiety, welcome it. If it brings you a tinge of despair, welcome it. And if it brings a ripple of insecurity, welcome it as well.
Each Obstacle that surfaces is an opportunity:

ul: To notice something alive within you right now.
To Validate, Normalize, Imagine, and Invite
To build the strength of your vagal brake, increasing your capacity for further self-regulation.

blocks.p: Imagine your self-regulation journey as a creek, and Obstacles as the rocks in it. Those rocks might be piled so high they've created a dam, and now your self-regulation flow is halted or slowed. Your goal is to clear the rocks from the creek and restore the flow of self-regulation.
"So, how do I get rid of the rocks?" You get rid of the rocks… by not getting rid of the rocks. I know, I know, it's a frustrating non-answer, but I beg your patience. I'll explain.

As you know, we don't reject our experiences. This includes the Obstacles within us. We don't reject them. We don't banish them. We don't minimize them. The question, "How do I get rid of the rocks?" is a rejection of the Obstacle. By rejecting it, you only reinforce it. The rocks won't move.

Instead of rejecting, we learn to be with the rocks. We allow them to exist, while also remaining anchored in safety. This duality is what will allow the creek flow to resume. At first, the self-regulation creek flow may only trickle through the rocks, but over time, it will flow more steadily. Over time, a rock may loosen, allowing more flow. Over time, the rocks may very slowly erode into sand and drift quietly downstream. Over time, the rocks may smooth out and loosen from each other further. Over time, self-regulation will increase.

blocks.why: Being with the rocks starts from safety. This practice anchors you first.

blocks.p: In essence, you give the rocks permission to remain, then pay attention to them. Your mindful, anchored attention to the rocks is what will open further self-regulation. How do you permit and pay attention to them? Through the skills: the ones you've already learned and the ones that come next.

ul: "I feel sad, and that makes sense given my life context. Sadness feels like a wet blanket draped over the back of my chair. It can be with me while I also take one mindful breath and reconnect with my senses."

"A self-defeating judgment entered my mind. I was taught self-defeating judgments early in life, so it makes sense I would think this way now. This thought looks like a blindfolded boxer. I'll place it in my pocket, and it can be with me as I take a walk."

blocks.p: There are more skills for welcoming and compassionately connecting with Obstacles ([Balancing and Pendulating](piece:balancing-and-pendulating)). For now, use what you have already learned when Obstacles surface during your practices: Validate, Normalize, Imagine, and Invite. As these become easier, apply the later skills.

While Obstacles will most definitely appear, how they show up is not certain. You might notice the same Obstacle emerging during each meditation practice. Over time, with repeated successful connections, it will lessen in intensity and become easier to welcome. You could also encounter multiple Obstacles surfacing one after another in a single meditation.

Focus on the most present-moment experience; pay attention to the Obstacle that feels most alive right now. This is your gateway to deeper self-regulation. It's okay to shift your focus as new Obstacles emerge; being flexible is essential.

Your body knows more than your conscious mind, right? So listen to it. Follow it. As your safety state holds, these "Obstacles" will guide you through self-regulation, and you just need to be aware of them as they come up.
"Obstacles keep piling up!"

Welcome to the onion-peeling process. This is completely normal, especially for long-standing, layered trauma. Work with the most present Obstacle. If a new one surfaces, shift to it as long as you are within your capacity. Repeat.
"The same Obstacle shows up every time I practice."

Recurring Obstacles are common and highlight what needs the most attention. Treat this as a priority for your nervous system. This Obstacle might be the key to deeper regulation. Keep working with it patiently. As you build capacity, it will eventually soften or shift.
"I Validate and Normalize, but the Obstacle won't leave!"

The goal isn't elimination: it's permitting and feeling within capacity. When you can be with the Obstacle without dysregulation, that's success. It might soften over time or reveal something underneath. Keep practicing. The point is to build your capacity to stay present with whatever arises.
"I feel like Obstacles mean I'm failing at meditation."

Obstacles are not failures; they're opportunities and often signs of progress. They surface because your safety state is strong enough to begin releasing what's been held. An Obstacle-free meditation isn't the goal. The goal is a meditation where you can notice, allow, and stay curious about the present moment whatever it brings, including Obstacles.

Obstacles are unexpected internal experiences that arise during practice. They are opportunities that indicate your vagal brake is releasing, that your safety state needs strengthening, or that dysregulation is surfacing.
Work with Obstacles by using Validating, Normalizing, Imagery, and Invitation to access the most present-moment experience. Use the later skills as your capacity allows.
Obstacles reveal layers of defense. As you address one layer, another may surface beneath it, which is typical and expected given the "onion-peeling" nature of self-regulation.
During your next practice session, when an Obstacle appears (and one probably will), pause and use the skills you have to welcome it:

ul: Imagine & Invite the Obstacle to be present while you reconnect with safety or do something else.

blocks.prompt: As Obstacles surface during practice, are you able to work with them or do they derail you?
Does reframing Obstacles as opportunities change how you relate to them?
Are you able to focus on the most present Obstacle?

blocks.h: The present moment and all it brings

blocks.p: Remember when I said [we're weird](piece:recovery-after-practice)? If it didn't click then, I sincerely hope it has now.
Now you see just how far outside the norm we are. It's usually at this point that clients and students realize how "weird" this is.

When I say we welcome the present moment mindfully, whatever it brings, this is what it looks like. We don't reject our internal experiences. We don't try to control them. We welcome them, both the pleasant and the unpleasant, the clear path and the Obstacles.
Of course, this is easier said than done. It gets easier over time with practice. You'll stumble and struggle. You'll feel insecure and doubt.
Have you ever heard the saying, "The way out is through," or some variation of it? It's a concept that appears in Buddhist and Stoic philosophy, and probably in others I am unaware of.
It's true. The way out is through.

Do you need to overcome grief? The way out is through. You must ultimately feel it in the present moment to "overcome" it. The same applies to anxiety, anger, or any emotion you're facing. But, as you know, we do this first from a place of safety. When we're anchored in safety and connected to the present, we lovingly greet defense. That's the "through" part of "the way out is through." To get out of defense, we go through it while anchored in safety.

But more broadly, to connect with the present moment as a baseline, we also need to experience it. Not only with safety, but also with whatever the present moment brings to our awareness. Repeating this process helps establish a general present-moment connection as a baseline in our daily life. Perfect and continuous? No, not exactly. But a higher baseline. More of a sense of connection than disconnection.
